relearning.title: Read: meiosis and sexual reproduction
relearning.description: A short reading with the pairs-of-shoes analogy, worked examples and quick checks.

body.text:
**I can model meiosis and discuss its importance in sexual reproduction.**

**Think of pairs of shoes.** Your closet has 23 pairs of shoes, 46 shoes in all, and in each pair one shoe came from mom and one from dad. Now pack a bag with exactly one shoe from every pair: 23 shoes. That is what meiosis does. A body cell has 23 **pairs** of chromosomes (46). A **gamete** (sperm or egg) gets **one from each pair** (23).

**Why it matters:** when a sperm (23) fertilizes an egg (23), the first cell of the baby, the **zygote**, has 23 + 23 = **46**. Without meiosis, the chromosome number would double every generation.

**Key words:**
**Diploid (2n):** two sets of chromosomes, like body cells (46 in humans).
**Haploid (n):** one set, like gametes (23 in humans).
**Homologous chromosomes:** a matching pair, one from each parent, with the same genes.

**The process:** the DNA is copied once, then the cell divides **twice**. **Meiosis I** separates the homologous pairs. **Meiosis II** separates the sister chromatids. Result: **4 haploid cells**, all genetically different.

**Worked example:** A fruit fly has 2n = 8. Its gametes have n = 8 ÷ 2 = **4** chromosomes.

checks.prompt: A human body cell has 46 chromosomes. How many chromosomes does a human egg cell have? Type a number.
checks.explanation: Meiosis halves the number: 46 ÷ 2 = 23. 46 is the body-cell (diploid) number, which is the common mistake.
Meiosis divides twice, making 4 haploid cells that are all different. 2 identical diploid cells is what mitosis makes, the common mix-up.

sections.title: Where the variety comes from

body.text:
**Mitosis vs. meiosis:**
Mitosis: 1 division, 2 identical diploid cells, for growth and repair.
Meiosis: 2 divisions, 4 different haploid cells, for making gametes.

**Crossing over** happens in **prophase I**. Homologous chromosomes pair up tightly and swap pieces, like two friends trading a few songs between their playlists. Each chromosome ends up with a new mix of mom's and dad's genes.

**Independent assortment** happens when the pairs line up in metaphase I. Each pair lines up in a random direction, so each gamete gets a random mix of mom's and dad's chromosomes. In humans that alone gives over 8 million (2^{23}) combinations.

**Why it matters:** this **genetic variation** is why brothers and sisters with the same parents look different (except identical twins). Variation helps a species survive when its environment changes.

**Worked example 2:** A dog has 2n = 78. Gametes: 78 ÷ 2 = **39**. After fertilization, the zygote has 39 + 39 = **78**.

**Worked example 3:** If chromosomes fail to separate in meiosis (**nondisjunction**), a gamete can end up with 24 or 22 chromosomes. A 24-chromosome egg fertilized by a normal sperm makes a zygote with 47, as in Down syndrome (an extra chromosome 21).

**Watch out for:** saying meiosis makes 2 cells (it makes 4), saying gametes are diploid (they are haploid), confusing homologous chromosomes (a pair, one from each parent) with sister chromatids (two copies made in the S phase), and putting crossing over in prophase II (it is prophase I).

checks.prompt: Crossing over happens during which phase?
checks.explanation: Crossing over happens in prophase I, when the homologous chromosomes are paired up. In meiosis II the partners have already separated, so prophase II is the common wrong answer.

checks.prompt: A cat has 38 chromosomes in its body cells. How many chromosomes are in each of its sperm cells? Type a number.
checks.explanation: Sperm are haploid: 38 ÷ 2 = 19. Answering 38 forgets that meiosis halves the number.

sections.shortAnswer: Explain two ways meiosis makes each gamete genetically different, and why that variation is important.

relearning.title: Do: flip the key terms, then follow a cell through meiosis
relearning.description: Flashcards with a 3-question self-quiz, then a cell with 2n = 4 followed through meiosis one step at a time.

cards.back: Cell division that makes gametes: 2 divisions, 4 haploid cells, all genetically different.
A sex cell: sperm or egg. Haploid (23 chromosomes in humans).
Two sets of chromosomes, like body cells. 46 in humans.
One set of chromosomes, like gametes. 23 in humans.
A matching pair, one from each parent, with the same genes. Like a pair of shoes.
Homologous chromosomes swap pieces in prophase I, mixing the genes.

checks.explanation: Gametes have one set of chromosomes, so they are haploid. Body cells are diploid, which is the common mix-up.

checks.prompt: A fruit fly has 2n = 8. How many chromosomes are in its gametes?
checks.explanation: Gametes are haploid: 8 ÷ 2 = 4. Doubling to 16 is the common mistake.

options.text: Two haploid gametes join to make a diploid zygote
Two diploid cells join to make a haploid cell

checks.explanation: A haploid sperm and a haploid egg join, so the zygote is diploid (23 + 23 = 46 in humans). Splitting into four is meiosis, not fertilization.

body.problem: Follow one cell with 2n = 4 (two homologous pairs: one long pair and one short pair) through meiosis.

steps.text: **Interphase:** every chromosome is copied. The cell still has 4 chromosomes, but each one is now two sister chromatids.
**Prophase I:** the homologous chromosomes pair up (long with long, short with short). Crossing over swaps pieces between the partners.
**Metaphase I and anaphase I:** the pairs line up in the middle in a random direction, then the partners separate. Each side gets one long and one short chromosome.
**Telophase I and cytokinesis:** 2 cells, each with 2 chromosomes (n = 2). Each chromosome still has two chromatids.
**Meiosis II:** in each cell, the chromosomes line up and the sister chromatids are pulled apart, just like in mitosis.
**Result:** 4 haploid cells, each with 2 chromosomes (one long, one short), and each with a different mix of genes.

checks.prompt: Your turn: what separates in anaphase I?
checks.explanation: Meiosis I separates the homologous pairs, and meiosis II separates the sister chromatids. Mixing up which division splits what is the common mistake.

checks.prompt: Your turn: a cell with 2n = 12 goes through meiosis. How many chromosomes are in each of the 4 cells at the end? Type a number.
checks.explanation: Each cell is haploid: 12 ÷ 2 = 6. Dividing by 4 because there are 4 cells (to get 3) is the common mistake.

checks.prompt: A human sperm with 23 chromosomes fertilizes an egg with 23 chromosomes. How many chromosomes does the zygote have? Type a number.
checks.explanation: 23 + 23 = 46. Meiosis halves the number first, so fertilization brings it back to 46 instead of doubling it every generation.

checks.prompt: Your closet has 23 pairs of shoes. In the shoe analogy, what does meiosis pack into each gamete?

options.text: Any 23 shoes, even if two come from the same pair
Exactly one shoe from every pair

checks.explanation: A gamete gets one chromosome from each homologous pair, so 23 in all. It is not just any 23: every pair has to be represented once.

sections.title: Meiosis: Why Are All Humans Unique?: Crash Course Biology #30

options.text: Homologous chromosomes pair up and swap pieces
The DNA is copied a second time

checks.explanation: Homologous chromosomes swap pieces, so each one ends up with a new mix of mom's and dad's genes. The DNA is only copied once in meiosis.

checks.prompt: In metaphase I, each homologous pair lines up in a random direction, so each gamete gets a random mix of mom's and dad's chromosomes. What is this called?
checks.explanation: Random lining up of the pairs is independent assortment. Crossing over is the swapping of pieces in prophase I, which is the common mix-up.

sections.shortAnswer: Explain why brothers and sisters with the same parents don't look identical. Use the words crossing over and independent assortment.
